title: Windowed batching vs Opportunistic slots — Latency & cost playbook
body:
Executive summary:

This note compares two scheduling/packing strategies we use in the serving runtime when request arrival patterns are bursty or session-centric: windowed batching (time-slicing requests into fixed short windows to build larger batches) and opportunistic slots (reserve small goroutines/slots that greedily fill from a small queue and flush on slot-full or timeout).

Motivation: customers frequently report tradeoffs between 1) predictable low p50 latency for short chat turns and 2) amortized token cost across many small requests. Our goal is to produce a concise decision guide with measured latency percentiles, token-unit cost delta, and operational knobs for SLOs.

Key takeaways (TL;DR):
- Windowed batching wins for cost at moderate-to-high request concurrency (>= 20 concurrent users per GPU) with small extra p50 (~5–12 ms) and modest p99 tail increase if window <= 10ms.
- Opportunistic slots give lower immediate p50 (~10–20% reduction) for extremely latency-sensitive routes (interactive search, per-keystroke experiences) but cost per token increases ~8–30% depending on observed slot fill rate.
- Combining both (adaptive policy: opportunistic for VIP/premium routes + windowed for bulk) yields best trade-offs for mixed workloads.

Methodology:
- Hardware: 8x A100-80GB (nvlink disabled for isolation), runtime compiled with TF32/GEMM kernels for 16k context.
- Models: open-llama-13B (fp16 baseline) and a quantized 13B-int8 variant used for cost comparisons.
- Workloads: synthesized session workloads to mimic chat product: 70% short-turns (8–32 tokens), 20% medium (50–120 tokens), 10% long (300–1024 tokens). Arrival patterns: Poisson baseline and microburst traces (bursts of 150–400 reqs/sec for 200–800ms) captured from customer traces.
- Batching policies tested:
  * windowed batching (W): time windows of 2ms, 5ms, 10ms, 25ms
  * opportunistic slots (S): slot counts 4, 8, 16 per GPU; flush timeout 3ms and 10ms
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency per request (wall clock), per-token CPU/GPU utilization, per-token $ cost (model+infra amortized), KV-cache hit rate, and number of kernel launches.

ASCII result tables (aggregated per 1M tokens):

1) Latency percentiles (model: 13B fp16; workload: mixed short/medium/long; concurrency: 25 active users/GPU; microburst pattern)

| Policy | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | avg tokens/sec/GPU |
|--------|----------|----------|----------|--------------------|
| W-2ms  | 48       | 120      | 220      | 45k                |
| W-5ms  | 53       | 135      | 260      | 54k                |
| W-10ms | 61       | 160      | 320      | 62k                |
| W-25ms | 80       | 240      | 480      | 70k                |
| S-4    | 44       | 140      | 400      | 39k                |
| S-8    | 42       | 130      | 360      | 46k                |
| S-16   | 40       | 125      | 340      | 52k                |

Notes: W-* shows predictable throughput increase with window size; p99 grows nonlinearly once windows exceed ~10ms. S-* yields lower p50 in many cases but p99 inflation is sensitive to slot starvation during microbursts.

2) Cost delta per 1M tokens (normalized to W-2ms = 100). Includes amortized GPU time + infra overheads (scheduling, kernel launches).

| Policy | Cost index (lower is better) |
|--------|-----------------------------|
| W-2ms  | 100                         |
| W-5ms  | 92                          |
| W-10ms | 84                          |
| W-25ms | 78                          |
| S-4    | 118                         |
| S-8    | 110                         |
| S-16   | 105                         |

Interpretation: larger windows lower cost by increasing GPU utilization and batching efficiency. Opportunistic slots pay a premium because many slots flush underfilled during rapid short-turn workloads, increasing kernel overhead and lowering amortization.

3) KV-cache hit sensitivity (short-turn heavy workload; cache hit increases effective tokens by reusing prefixes)

| Policy | kv-hit (%) | effective cost index |
|--------|------------|----------------------|
| W-5ms  | 28         | 78                   |
| S-8    | 32         | 86                   |
| hybrid | 35         | 70                   |

Observation: opportunistic slots can sometimes enable higher KV reuse because they co-locate turns from the same session more often; hybrid routing (session-affinity + windowed batching for anonymous traffic) gets the best of both worlds.

Operational considerations / failure modes:
- Head-of-line blocking: large windows can cause short urgent requests to wait; mitigate with priority lanes (always-run slots for <10-token requests).
- Slot starvation: during sudden bursts, opportunistic slots that are occupied by long-turns can block short-turns; enforce slot preemption or fast-eviction policy.
- Kernel launch overhead: many small batches increase kernel-launch overhead and host-to-device transfers; measured overhead accounted for in cost index.
- Cold-start warmup: longer windows slightly increase probability of cold-model invocations per batch start; pre-warming critical for low-latency SLOs.

Example decision matrix (simple):
- If p50 SLO < 60ms and cost sensitivity high -> W-2ms or S-8 depending on concurrency and KV patterns.
- If p50 SLO < 40ms (very aggressive) and customer on premium tier -> S-16 with reserved slots + pre-warm and session-affinity.
- If target is cost minimization with p99 SLO <= 300ms -> W-10ms with adaptive window increase during low traffic.

Recommendations (practical knobs):
1) Launch an "adaptive-batcher" feature flag: starts with W-5ms and switches to W-10ms if observed concurrency > 40 per GPU for >30s.
2) Expose two route-level knobs to customers: scheduling_policy = {windowed, opportunistic, hybrid} and slot_budget (integer). Default remains windowed for free tier.
3) Implement per-slot preemption: long-run requests occupying unusual time slices can be moved to background drain after X ms if slot starvation observed.
4) Add telemetry: metric slot_fill_rate, average_flush_size, kernel_launchs_per_1k_tokens, and per-route kv_affinity_rate. These should be surfaced in Console Optimize as recommended actions.
5) Promoted best-practice: hybrid default for chat endpoints where session-affinity exists; opportunistic for search/autocomplete endpoints with strict p50 needs.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Repeat the same matrix with the quantized 13B-int8 variant to measure cost amplification under quantization (we expect S-* penalty to shrink due to lower per-kernel cost).
- Run at scale across regions (europe + us-west) to verify network latency interaction with window timers.
- A/B test adaptive-batcher with 10 paying customers (mix of PLG and enterprise) to measure real-world slot fill rates and customer-perceived latency.

Appendix: example microburst trace (text):
Burst start: t=0ms, peak QPS=360, sustained 200ms, decay 500ms. Inter-burst idle 2s.
Trace snippet (requests per 10ms): 0,0,0,10,32,78,120,150,130,90,60,30,12,2,0,0

Simple ASCII sparkline for p50 vs policy (lower better):
W-2ms: ████▉
W-5ms: █████▉
W-10ms: ███████
W-25ms: ███████████
S-4: ████
S-8: ████▊
S-16: ███▉

Questions / open issues:
- Should we provide a managed "latency-preservation" addon that guarantees p50 for a set of routes using reserved opportunistic slots? Pricing model TBD.
- How aggressive should preemption be without creating thrash? Need simulation and production canary.
- Does slot preemption interact badly with KV-cache affinity (we could evict useful cache locality)? Evaluate with session-aware eviction policy.
